tldr: Stale workaround comments spread because coding agents copy them
summary: Argues you should delete most code comments, because coding agents copy existing workaround comments and spread hacks through the codebase. Suggests pstack's /no-comments skill to prune useless ones.
text:
ban and delete most if not all code comments!

agents love copying what already exists. a seemingly harmless comment explaining some temporary workaround is one of the worst viruses you can have in your codebase. like a weed it'll spread quickly as a tool for agents to quickly get their job done. before you know it, your codebase is overrun with hacks and stale comments. just one more workaround bro 

you can use pstack's /no-comments skill as a weedkiller. it'll seek out useless comments while keeping the ones that actually should exist (like explaining a browser quirk), and figure out how to solve them on a first principles basis

here's a prompt you can try asking @bot:

create a project agent that uses /poteto-mode to spawn a /swarm to use /no-comments and identify useless code comments we can prune in my repo. come back with a high level plan of which of these workarounds would be best solved by refactoring and which we can straight up delete

https://t.co/nqeRdY62ee
key_points: Agents imitate existing code, so stale workaround comments spread like weeds.
Keep only comments that must exist, such as browser-quirk explanations.
pstack's /no-comments skill finds useless comments and plans refactor vs. delete.
action: Have an agent run /no-comments on one repo and sort each comment into refactor or delete.

tldr: Jev injects image tokens so models can ask with images
summary: TypeSafe's Jev launch shows decision models that ask questions with images by replacing asset references with raw image tokens at inference. The thread covers vibe-sensitive visual reasoning (e.g. tarot), token-efficient image placement in state vs the question, and decomposing multi-step visual tasks.
text:
New @typesafeai Jev capabilities!
 
Some decision models can ask questions about images but can they ask questions with images?

🧵 How to get the most out of the new Jev launch https://t.co/kXIg0M9jqo

Jev gets vibes, it is trained to pick up on subtle signals.

Jev knows the tarot is a visual language of associations.

The 3rd question is especially interesting, each `asset reference` is replaced at inference time with the raw image tokens. The model doesn't see the word https://t.co/uvfphw0Zst

Because the TypeSafe's system injects the images with a string replace, it is important to tune your questions and state for token efficiency. If you reuse an image you can put it in the state, but if it's question local, keep it there.

More token efficiency, more intelligence https://t.co/ZYaZbceO3U

Here I am proud of Jev, it unpacks:

- What is the last item?
- What does it mean to map onto the strip
- What PH is a `lemon`
- Where is that PH on the strip

We recommend decomposing questions because each step adds difficulty - Nice job little buddy! https://t.co/ui5m50Osca

Hat's off to our  designer at @typesafeai  (they prefer to create behind the scenes)!

Fast turnaround with the whole team <3
key_points: Asset references are swapped for raw image tokens at inference, so the model never sees the placeholder word.
Put reused images in state; keep one-off images in the question for token efficiency.
Decompose hard visual questions into steps; each step adds difficulty.
Jev is trained to pick up subtle visual associations, not only literal labels.
action: Put reused images in Jev state and keep question-local ones in the question.

tldr: Make agent work trustworthy by fixing the codebase before adding rules
summary: Lays out an inverse pyramid for trusting coding agents: put most effort into codebase design, then static analysis, then prose rules, and least into human review. The post invites readers to hand it to their bot or agent, and ends with a pstack prompt for a Project that studies your past feedback and proposes a more agent-friendly rearchitecture.
text:
how do you trust your agents' work more? copy this post/link and give it to your @bot or agent!

1. codebase improvements: this is just good software engineering - better architecture, stronger types and invariants, clear boundaries. agents love to copy what exists and take the shortest path, so make the easy thing the right thing. categorically eliminate problems through code and you won't need to think about it again.
2. static analysis: lint rules, tests, CI, verification (eg TLA+). very token efficient ways to catch issues ahead of time.
3. prose: comments, rules, AGENTS.md, skills - anything that can't be enforced and requires agent judgment. use it minimally, but do use /create-verification-skill.
4. human review: the hardest to scale. at the rate agents land code, it's pretty much impossible to thoroughly review every PR, so spend that effort on the highest leverage point, designing an environment where agents do the right thing by default.

this forms an inverse pyramid: you want most of your effort at the top, least at the bottom. codebase improvements are deterministic, making it more token efficient, and lets you sleep more soundly at night.

install https://t.co/u9xIlN3eN0 and create a new Project:
1. look through my slack/chat messages and code review comments where i've given feedback on PRs, code, architecture
2. use /recall on my past transcripts to learn how i steer agents
3. /poteto-mode use /correct and /architect on past commits to find the most common pitfalls agents fall into, then propose a plan to rearchitect the code i own so it's more agent friendly. answer open questions with prototyping rather than defer to me, and back the plan with real data. 
4. before you begin, use /sharpen + /in-your-own-words and confirm this prompt with me
key_points: Agents copy what exists and take the shortest path, so make the easy path the correct one in code.
Lint rules, tests, CI and formal verification catch problems cheaply before review.
Keep prose rules like AGENTS.md and skills minimal, for judgment calls code can't enforce.
Human review doesn't scale with agent output, so spend it on designing the environment.
action: Install pstack and start a Project that runs /recall, /correct and /architect on your history to propose an agent-friendly rearchitecture, confirmed first with /sharpen.

tldr: How the Claude Code team reviews code at agent-scale volume
summary: With Claude writing about 90% of Claude Code's code, the team moved most review to layered automated checks and risk-tiered human approval, doubling merged PRs from June to September while the revert share fell over 40%. The linked post explains each layer and how other teams can adopt it.
text:
Claude writes about 90% of Claude Code's code.

From June to September, merged PRs more than doubled while the share reverted fell by more than 40%.

We wrote about how we changed code review to get there, and how to adopt it:

https://t.co/9sZe64g3mb
key_points: Review runs continuously before a PR exists: the agent must show test or build output, then a fresh-context subagent reviews the diff.
AI findings are verified by other agents voting before posting, and every finding must be fixed or resolved with a reason.
Human approvals scale by risk tier set from the change, not the author, and a bot approval never replaces a required human.
Cap review rounds and switch to diff-only re-review, since agent reviewers otherwise keep re-finding old bugs.
action: Add a short REVIEW.md to one repo listing what failure looks like there, then run /code-review locally before your next PR.

tldr: A practical tutorial on being more ambitious with AI models
summary: Felix Rieseberg, an eng lead on Claude, turns the vague advice to be more ambitious with AI into a tutorial with four kinds of ambition and concrete prompts for each. It matters because it shows how to move models from small tasks to outcomes, expert-level depth, and cross-field ideas.
text:
Hi, I'm Felix. I'm an eng lead working on Claude. I love watching people take flight and do things they never thought possible.

We often describe that as "being more ambitious" when using AI, which is tricky advice to follow. I wrote a tutorial:

https://t.co/vNPPs5FWm8
key_points: Altitude: ask for the goal beyond the task, like keeping apps crash-free instead of fixing one crash.
Depth: insist on the tools real experts use, set unreasonable targets, and check results with an outside judge, not the model itself.
Range: pull in other fields, for example by describing the work as verbs instead of nouns.
Higher-level workflows often need setup first, such as giving the model crash reports and machines to verify fixes.
action: Before your next big prompt, ask the model what a top professional would do differently, which raw data and methods they'd use, then rewrite the prompt.

tldr: Replace line-by-line code review with layered automated verification for agents
summary: Argues that when agents write code faster than humans can review it, the bottleneck becomes proving it works, so review should evolve into a multi-layered verification system. It points to the Claude Code team, where Claude writes 90%+ of the code, as proof that heavy investment in verification keeps speed without losing stability.
text:
Give your agent a way to verify its work. This can dramatically improve the quality of output.

With this process in place, Claude Code was able to write 90%+ of its code itself. When generating software at a faster rate than you can review it, the bottleneck shifts to proving that it works. @bcherny and team invested enough in verification, we've been able to move fast while maintaining stability.

Code reviews aren't going away, but you need to think of it differently. One human reading through line-by-line is no longer going to work as a gate, it needs to evolve into a multi-layered verification system, built with fast deterministic feedback loops for your agents. 

This is where e2e tests, feature maps (as @poteto has been advocating), property tests and multi-agent adversarial reviews come in. These all provide opportunities to catch errors early and fix them before things get out of hand.

You don't have enough eyeballs for the amount of code being written so your focus needs to be on product intent, risk assessment and evaluating evidence rather than reviewing code. Delegate the code checking work to your automated tests, scale your approvals based on risk, and turn your test failures into living evaluations. This approach helps maintain speed without losing reliability.

Let the agents do what they do best and let you focus on what makes you irreplaceable: judgement, direction, and ownership. We tried to capture how we handle code review and verification in this writeup. Hopefully it's helpful.
key_points: Giving agents a way to verify their own work sharply improves output quality.
A single human reading line by line can't gate agent-speed code; build fast deterministic feedback loops instead.
Layer e2e tests, feature maps, property tests and multi-agent adversarial reviews to catch errors early.
Humans should focus on product intent, risk assessment and evidence, scaling approvals by risk.
action: Add one fast verification layer to an agent-heavy repo, such as e2e tests or a feature map, and have the agent run it before every handoff.

tldr: Split work by whether AI can verify it, then adjust how you work
summary: Lee Knowlton argues that how you use AI should depend on whether AI can check its own output: verifiable work can be handed off at scale, borderline work needs an AI judge backed by evals, and unverifiable work still needs your focused attention. A flowchart lays out the decision.
text:
notes on using AI productively:

- you can separate most work into two buckets: AI-verifiable and not. how you should work depends on which bucket your work falls into

- "verifiable" boils down to whether AI can independently tell (verify) if work that it completes is good or not.

- if your work is verifiable, design a verifier or system of verifiers and "let 'er rip." use as much AI as you can and get out of the way. you're not the bottleneck anymore, so no marginal attention is required as tasks scale.

- if it might be verifiable, you can try building an AI judge. but you need evals to test the judge's competence. @hammer_mt is my go-to on how to do this well. if you can get your judge good enough, you have verifiable work. back to throwing as much ai at your work as you can

- sometimes a good judge is easy to build, sometimes it's so hard that you may as well not bother.

- if your work can't be verified by an AI, that leaves you or someone else as the judge. treat it like the olden days but with AI help. one or two tasks at a time, avoid context switching, protect your focus

- sometimes, there are verifiable sub-tasks within larger pieces of work. The same process re: judgment and eval-building applies to these sub-tasks. The more you can automate these away, the more you can focus on the pieces that you're uniquely suited for.
key_points: If AI can verify the result, build verifiers and let it run at scale without your attention.
If it might be verifiable, build an AI judge and test it with evals before trusting it.
If only a human can judge, work the old way with AI help: one or two tasks, no context switching.
Pull verifiable sub-tasks out of larger work and automate them so you focus on what only you can do.
action: List your current tasks and mark each as AI-verifiable, maybe, or not, then build a verifier or eval for one maybe task.

tldr: A four-quadrant map for developing mind, body, spirit, and vocation
summary: Dan Koe's X article lays out Human 3.0, a self-development model that maps your life across four quadrants (Mind, Body, Spirit, Vocation), each with three levels of consciousness, three phases of change, and traits you build to level up. He argues most models cover only one domain, and this one aims to show where you're stuck and which problem to solve next.
text: https://t.co/CdLm1xoOAb
key_points: The four quadrants, adapted from Ken Wilber's AQAL model, are Mind, Body, Spirit, and Vocation, and a problem in one is rarely solved by working on another.
Each quadrant has three levels (Conformist, Individualist, Synthesist), and you move up through Dissonance, Uncertainty, and Discovery phases.
Progress needs knowledge, experience, and skill together; knowing without practice leads to False Transformation, where you only imitate the next level.
Channels, obsessive rabbit holes of learning or building, are the fastest way through a Dissonance phase to the next level.

tldr: 只测用户能感知的行为：150个GPT用例抓到15个bug
summary: 作者说，公司一位有10年经验的DevOps花两个月给一个二十多万行的webapp生成了5000多个单元测试，只发现几个无关痛痒的bug；而且单元测试依赖实现，每次改代码都要删掉重生成，开发怨声载道。他接手后定下原则：只测用户能感知到的东西，不基于内部实现写测试，并写了一个通用测试技能，只让GPT生成150个用例就抓到15个bug。结论：一般产品不必再写单元测试，多人长期vibe coding的产品核心功能可能能用，但用户可见的边角bug率很高，需要专门的测试工作流。
text:
我们之前招的10年经验DevOps，也会自动化测试。花了2个月，给我们公司一个只有二十多万行的webapp产品，生成了5000多个单元测试。只查出来几不痛不痒的bug。
因为单元测试依赖于实现，每次开发们改代码，都要花几十分钟，删除老的单元测试，重新生成新的单元测试，怨声载道。
这个DevOps离职以后，我不让老板再招人，我自己接手这个自动化测试。我定了一个原则，测试用例只测用户能感知到的东西，绝对不基于任何内部实现写测试。我还写了一个通用测试技能，只让GPT生成150个测试用例，就抓到了15个bug。
我的结论是：一般的产品不要再写单元测试。多人长时间vibe coding出来的东西，可能核心功能能用，但是用户可见的边边角角的bug率非常高，如果没有专门的工作流去测试，很难发现。
key_points: 5000多个基于实现的单元测试只找到几个小bug，还拖慢每次改动。
原则：测试用例只覆盖用户可感知的行为，不依赖内部实现。
一个通用测试技能让GPT生成150个用例，抓到15个bug。
作者认为vibe coding产品的风险集中在用户可见的边角情况。

tldr: PHP脆弱性の後、CTOとCISOが今すぐ下すべき4つの判断
summary: GMO Flatt Securityの米内氏が、昨晩からのPHP脆弱性対応を受けて、AIによる脆弱性発見で年末まで高負荷が続くと予測し、CTO/CISOに4つの判断を求めています。新規開発を減らしてセキュリティに時間・予算を割きチームを休ませること、必要なら予防的なサービス停止を覚悟すること、平時にはメモリ安全でないレガシーの作り直しと廃止を進めること、そして役割のサイロを越えた総力戦です。
text:
【PHP脆弱性対応の「後」にむけて】

みなさん、昨晩からのPHP対応お疲れ様です。一晩中連絡鳴り止んでおらず、一部の個別メッセージに返せてなくて申し訳ないです。

一括して、今、世の中の CTOs/CISOs に届いてほしいことを４つ書き残しておきます↓

（まとまりない部分もあるのですが、投稿しないよりマシかなと、このまま投げちゃいます）

Point 1: これからは、ソフトウェア業界全体で、高負荷の続くタイミングになります。意図してセキュリティに時間をあて、チームが「休息」が取れる体制を。
・我々は脆弱性リサーチに数年間継続的に取り組んできてました。だからこそ感じますが、ここ一年（体感では GPT-5.6 Sol 以後）が、最も「本当に？」みたいな脆弱性が掘り出されていく一年になると思います。こんなのまだあったの？という驚きとともに。
・特に複雑なメモリバグの類（memory safe でない言語製のものを中心に）、あるいは認可バグの類が中心になると思われます。
・少なくともここから年末までは、このクラスの脆弱性がまだまだ出てくると考えておく必要があります。（僕が読み外しているかもしれませんが、恐らく高い確度でこうなります。直近のPHP脆弱性すら、いま世界中の研究者が Variant Analysis をしていて、多分まだ出てくるでしょう）
・このご時世では、新規機能の開発に割く時間を明確に落とすしかありません。あくまで経営者である CTO には取りにくい判断なのは重々承知です（僕もそうなので）。
・「対応AIで」と思うかも知れません。これは技術的には正しいです。ただ、組織的には正しくないです。確実になんとかならず、組織は疲弊していきます。
・なんせセキュリティ対応は大抵自分にタイミングが御せないからです。深夜の対応、急な対応、計画の変更、デグレへの不安、脆弱性情報過多（そもそも自社に影響があるかも分からないものが大半なのに）… と、ストレスの強度がぐんぐん高まっていきます。昨日〜今朝のPHP対応のようなものが、毎週あれば、チームは比較的簡単に壊れてしまうでしょう。
・敢えてリーダーが、セキュリティへの、時間・お金（・トークン）にアロケしてください。これは経営者にしか取れない択で、かついま技術経営者に求められることです。

Point 2: 「必要なら予防的にサービス停止」の覚悟を決め、予めできる調整を重ねたい。止められない場合は、仮想パッチ・監視へのリソースアロケを。
・前提、今回のPHPの件のような脆弱性の対応では、「顧客の保護のためならサービスを止めざるを得ない場面」が訪れます。今回も様々なビジネスがそれに直面しました。今後も訪れるでしょう。
・今回の経験を旨に、本当に止めてはならないのか、止めらるのか、止めうる期待値調整がお客様と出来ているか、を徹底的に見直しておきましょう。
・直近の流れをうけての、お客様への事前連絡（スタンス表明）も有効だと思います。（弊社 GMO Flatt Security 製品についても、これからそれをし、リリースノートとして掲示予定です。我々のサービスの侵害、特に Takumi Guard の侵害は、ソフトウェサプライチェーンの最悪な侵害につながるからです。）
・勿論、止めてはならないビジネスも様々存在します。ビジネスドメインに由来する規制/制約（特に金融・医療セグメント）もあれば、顧客とのSLAもあるでしょう。ただし、現代においては、それらに反するリスクと、セキュリティ被害にあうリスクを天秤にかける必要がでてきています。少し前まではサービス停止でのデメリットは容易に考えられても、セキュリティ侵害など考えにくい、という時代でしたが、今はそうではありません。この天秤を再考する必要があります。（なお、「もう何がなんでも止めてはならない」ビジネスは、相当に限定的だと思います。）
・どうしても止めてはならない（もう何がなんでも止めてはならないもの。限定的であれ存在。人命に関わるもの中心）という場合、厳しい戦いになりますが、WAFレイヤなどで緩和策を施しては祈り、監視する、という流れになります。必要なコンポーネント（WAFなど）と運用リソースがあるならば、苦しい時代ですが、休息うまく取りながらやっていきましょう。なければ、これもしんどいですが、整えましょう。

Point 3: もし平時があれば、システムのモダナイズ（Rebuild and Retire）を検討されたい。
・もし自社での緊急対応が落ち着いているならば、レガシーコンポーネント（数年塩漬けのシステム）、誰がメンテできるのか分からないオーパーツ的存在から順に、作り直し（Rebuild）と旧システムの廃止（Retire）を試みてください。新規開発の代わりに、ここにリソースを充てることが CTO/CISO の仕事です。（他の誰もそれを決められないので。）これは追々自分たちを助けてくれる（ついでにAI-native 開発に移行できて改善しやすくなる）とも思料。
・どのシステムからモダナイズしていくかですが：「XXXで書かれているとまずい」というのは燃えるし言いにくいものの、memory unsafe な言語、type safety があまり確保されていない言語の実装は、モダナイズを検討すべきでしょう。（僕はPHP好きですが、C/C++ で書かれた php-src は、やはりメモリバグ類に対して見通しに限界がありますね。好きなんですが…）
・また経験上、開発当時に DevOps プラクティスすら整っていなかった時代のソフトウェアも、モダナイズを検討したほうがよいです。「セキュリティ診断」をしても、取り返しのつかない量の脆弱性が出てきて、作り直したほうが早い、となる傾向にあります。（弊社でも診断/ペネトレしてますが、こうなると、どうしようもありません。）
・ただし Rebuild には、強いソフトウェア開発力が必要で、AI-native なスタイルに移行することは必須です。この意味で CTO の力がいります。かつ、どこからレガシーの追い出しをするか、どうレキュリティ的なレジリエンスを確保するかは、CISO 的な感性が求められます。既製品（とくに SaaS）を買って処理したほうがいいな、というような判断には CIO 的センスが求められます。総力戦だと思ってください。

Point 4: CTO/CISO の総力戦を。
・Point 3でも述べた通り、直近のくだりには、CTO/CISO の総力戦が必要です。ボードがセキュリティに向かって一致団結する必要があります。
・結構これらロールの間にサイロがあるケースがありますが、そんなことを言っている場合ではありません。
・団結を！
key_points: ここから年末までは複雑なメモリバグや認可バグが次々に見つかる前提で、新規機能開発の時間を意図的に減らす。
「AIで対応」は技術的には正しくても組織は疲弊する。リーダーが時間・お金・トークンをセキュリティに割り当て、休息を確保する。
顧客保護のための予防的サービス停止を覚悟し、顧客と期待値を調整しておく。止められないならWAFなどの仮想パッチと監視に資源を回す。
平時には塩漬けのレガシーやmemory unsafeな言語の実装からRebuild and Retireを進め、CTO/CISO/CIOが総力戦で動く。
action: 自社サービスごとに、重大脆弱性の際に予防停止できるか、止められない場合のWAF・監視体制があるかを一覧にする。

tldr: Ask agents for diagrams, recordings and specs, not PR summaries
summary: Ben Holmes argues that asking agents for text summaries of a pull request wastes what they can do. Better artifacts: architecture diagrams that explain the change visually (ASCII, Mermaid, HTML or animated walkthroughs; /show-me is a starting point), screen recordings that verify the change end to end, which most harnesses can now make with Chrome DevTools or computer use, and planning documents checked in as code when humans were in the loop. A product spec with the purpose and expected user flow both guides the agent toward better recorded verification and helps reviewers reading someone else's work. He notes Warp Factories links all artifacts from an agent session and can auto-edit the videos.
text:
Stop asking agents for text summaries of a PR. They're capable of so much more:

- Architecture diagrams to visually explain the change. Could be ascii, mermaid, HTML, or animated walkthroughs. /show-me is a great starting point.
- Screen recordings verifying the change end-to-end. Most harnesses can do this now with Chrome DevTools or computer use. Warp Factories will auto-edit video and highlight cursor clicks as well.
- Planning documents when humans were in the loop, checked in as code. This is optional, but a product spec explaining the purpose and expected user flow will a) guide the agent to better screen recording verification, and b) help the reviewer when looking at another engineer's work.

Warp Factories shows all artifacts connected to an agent session to make these easy to find.
key_points: Diagrams explain the change faster than prose.
A screen recording is end-to-end proof the change works.
Check in a short spec: it guides the agent and the reviewer.
action: On your next agent PR, ask for a Mermaid diagram of the change and a screen recording of the user flow instead of a summary.

tldr: Ryo Lu: don't let AI remove the struggle that teaches
summary: Ryo Lu's essay "struggle together". He learned programming and design by trying, failing and trying again, until hard-won lessons "became like water". Now we can ask a machine: he has made things with these tools he might never have made otherwise, but wonders what happens when we remove the difficulty before we understand what it was teaching us, since a result that looks complete hides the questions we never learned to ask. The other loss is people. Working with others is uncomfortable, but struggling together is how you become a band and how many of his closest friendships began. An always-patient agent can feel easier than reaching toward someone who might disagree, and those personal worlds run on company servers shaped by interests we may not see. He does not think pain makes things good, but wants tools that help us spend more time with the world and with each other instead of fewer reasons to enter it.
text:
struggle together

i learned programming and design by trying, failing, and trying again.

when i hit a wall, i figured out how to climb it. read something i barely understood. took things apart. asked someone for help. started over.

when i began my career, i kept doing things i had never done before. trying different ways to make something work. when i stopped learning, i moved on to the next struggle.

many things i made weren’t very good. but after enough rounds, something stuck. what once took so much effort became part of how i thought. i could feel something was wrong before i knew how to explain it.

it became like water.

i think about what went into that. the bug i couldn’t fix. the design that looked right until someone used it. the conversation that made me realize my flaws.

now we can ask a machine.

i’ve made things with these tools that i might never have made otherwise. i don’t miss every tedious task. but i wonder what happens when we remove the difficulty before we understand what it was teaching us.

we ask. something appears. it works well enough. we move on.

we learn how to get results without necessarily understanding how it works. and because the result looks complete, it becomes easy to miss the questions we never learned to ask.

there is another side to this.

working with people is uncomfortable.

everyone wants something different. everyone has a history you don’t know. someone cares about a detail you think is unimportant. someone pushes back when you want to move. someone needs time when you feel certain.

it takes a while to find each other.

but sometimes, after struggling together, you become a band.

you know who notices what you miss. who can pull an idea apart without killing it. when to step in, when to slow down, when to let someone else carry the rhythm.

you share something unfinished. admit you don’t know. hurt each other, apologize, try again. eventually you make something none of you could have made alone.

some of my closest friendships came from working this way. smart, caring humans who saw me confused, wrong, tired, excited. people i could be vulnerable with. people whose ideas changed mine.

i worry we are making it easier to avoid that beginning.

an agent is always there. patient. ready to keep going. talking to it can feel easier than reaching toward someone who might misunderstand you, disagree, or have somewhere else to be.

sometimes that ease helps. but if we keep choosing it, where do the friendships begin?

i picture each of us with our own agents. our own explanations. our own little worlds. making more things, with fewer reasons to leave the screen or work through a difference with another person.

and these worlds aren’t entirely ours.

they run on machines in server farms, owned by companies, shaped by interests we may not see. we bring them our questions, our work, our loneliness. they become part of how we understand what is real.

is that freedom?

or a comfortable kind of confinement, where everything responds to us but fewer things reach us?

i don’t think pain makes something good. there are struggles nobody should have to endure. but i don’t want to lose the difficulty of learning something unfamiliar, or getting to know someone who isn’t like me.

maybe we need tools that help us spend more time with the world, instead of giving us fewer reasons to enter it. tools that make it easier to find people, share something unfinished, and work through what we couldn’t figure out alone.

sometimes i want to close the laptop.

sit with people i love. play something we haven’t figured out yet. miss a note, lose the rhythm, listen until we find each other again.

like a jazz band. everyone bringing something different. nobody knowing where we’ll end up.

i don’t want a life without struggle. i want people to struggle with. something we can feel, change, and make our own.

music we couldn’t have made alone, instead of the silent static of the server farm.
key_points: Difficulty teaches things a finished-looking result hides.
Struggling together with people builds bands and friendships.
Want tools that send us toward the world, not away from it.
action: Next time you hit a wall, try one round with a person (or the docs) before asking the agent.

tldr: Nyxis: a Lean-verified backend framework that proves authorization safety
summary: banr1_ (NyxFoundation) released Nyxis, a backend framework written mostly in Lean. Its machine-checked theorem says that for any sequence of HTTP requests, no authenticated principal can read, change, delete or grant data beyond its rightful permissions. Developers only maintain the policy of who may do what, so the rest of the code can be left to AI agents without losing authorization safety. Unlike Microsoft and GitHub's PDD Kit, which needs a spec per program, Nyxis fixes the theorem in advance. The author is upfront about limits: code outside the proof and the runtime are trusted, a wrong policy gives no protection, and expressiveness and Lean libraries are still thin. He released early because of the recent wave of breaches. A reply points out that the assumptions file requires the database to be unreachable through Supabase's Data API or other apps; a second path around Nyxis is outside the proof.
text:
情報漏洩が起きないことを数学的に保証するバックエンドフレームワーク「Nyxis」を公開しました！

たぶん世界初です。

Nyxisで書かれたバックエンドは、企業の持つ機密情報をより安全に守ることができます。

昨今急増しているサイバー攻撃を防ぐ手段として、このような方法があることをお伝えしたいと思い、今回の発表に至りました。

開発者は「どの権限を持つユーザーが何を実行可能であるか」のルールを管理するだけで、残りのコードをAIエージェントに任せても認可の安全性が担保されます。

Nyxisは大部分がLean言語で記述されており、形式検証によって

「任意のHTTPリクエスト列に対し、認証された主体の正当な権限を逸脱するデータの読取・変更・削除・権限付与は発生しない」

という認可安全性定理を機械的に証明しています。

認可の不備は、OWASP脆弱性ランキングにおいて2019年版から連続1位であり、最優先で対策すべきリスクの一つです。

形式検証を活用したこのフレームワークは、テストに頼る従来の開発に比べて、格段にセキュアなソフトウェアを実現します。

先日MicrosoftとGitHubが、形式検証を用いた開発キット「PDD Kit」を発表しました。

こちらはより幅広い性質を扱える一方、プログラムごとに仕様を作り、それが意図に合っているかを開発者が確認する必要があります。

Nyxisは証明する定理を認可安全性に絞ってあらかじめ定めているため、開発者はポリシーを管理するだけで済みます。

もちろん、一定の仮定は存在しています。証明外コードと実行環境は信頼する前提であり、開発者がポリシーを誤って書けば、意図した保護は得られません。

この定理の範囲内において、数学的保証は非常に強力です。実システムに組み込める技術としてここまでの保証を与えたものは、私の知る限りまだ存在しません。

一方で、表現力の乏しさやLeanのライブラリ不足など、改善すべき点はまだ山積みです。

本当はもっと完成度が高まった時点で公開しようと考えていましたが、昨今のセキュリティインシデントの状況を鑑みて、このタイミングで発表することにしました。

世界をセキュアにする一助になれば嬉しいです。

https://t.co/p6fHK0KGwu
key_points: Authorization-safety theorem proved in Lean for any HTTP request sequence.
Developers write only the permission policy; agents can write the rest.
Trusted: code outside the proof, the runtime, and a correct policy.
The database must not be reachable another way, such as Supabase's Data API.
action: Read ASSUMPTIONS.md and check whether your database has a second path around the API

tldr: Huntley: build many little bots and pipe them together
summary: Geoffrey Huntley says the best way to use @bot is to create lots of little bots, Unix-style, and pipeline them together, which he calls basically reactive stream programming. His screenshot shows a chain: a bot asks a "Travel - Trips" bot where he is and when, then another pulls the week's gigs, shows, exhibitions and meetups in Singapore and trims the list once his flight date arrives. In a reply he says it surfaced an event with Evan You on Friday automatically, and he RSVPed.
text: the best way to use @bot is to create lots of little bots. think posix/unix composition. then pipeline them together. it’s basically reactive stream programming tbh. https://t.co/wHjH2JxDs6
key_points: Small single-purpose bots, composed like Unix pipes.
Each bot hands its output to the next, like a reactive stream.
His example: a trip bot feeds an events bot that trims by travel dates.
action: Split one big agent routine into two small bots and pipe one into the other

tldr: X's feed no longer cuts brand-new posts first
summary: Peter Mick reads X's open-sourced ranking code: the For You feed checks only 2,800 of about 3,700 candidates, and new posts used to be cut first; now every source is trimmed equally. Posts labeled low quality or misinfo get a warning and can't be liked or shared by non-followers.
text:
X ALGORITHM UPDATE 🚨

X just stopped cutting new posts first, and that should help small accounts (I check it daily with Claude and share updates worth sharing with you)

tl;dr:

- X can only check 2,800 posts each time you open your feed
- new posts used to be last in line, so they got cut first
- now everything gets cut equally, new posts included
- posts labeled low quality or misinfo now show a warning, and people can't like, reply or share them
- no score changes this time

lesson learned: your new posts now get a fair chance to be seen. Your first 2 hours still matter most.

full details:

- How it worked until this week

Every time someone opens For You, X collects around 3,700 posts it could show them: posts from people they follow, popular posts, posts liked by similar people, and brand new posts.

But X only has time to check 2,800 of them.

So it just took the first 2,800 in line. Brand new posts were at the back of the line. When there were too many, they were the ones left out... and a post that never gets checked can't be shown.

- What changed

Now everything gets cut by the same amount. 25% too many? Every type of post loses 25%, new posts included. Nobody goes first.

- Why small accounts should care

Those brand new posts are under 2 hours old, with under 8 likes and under 500 views. That's where most posts from smaller accounts are.

My read: they now get a fair chance instead of being cut first. How often X actually hits the 2,800 limit isn't in the code, so I can't tell you how big the difference is.

- Low quality and misinfo posts now show a warning

If X labels your post as low quality or misinformation, people who don't follow you see a warning on it, and they can't like, reply, repost, bookmark or share it. The code doesn't say what gets a post that label.

Here's a recap of what you should be doing:

- a new post gets its extra push only in its first 2 hours and first 200 views, so post when your people are online
- likes carry more weight than ever at 0.66 each
- people sticking around pays, the time-spent score is 50% higher than two weeks ago
- a read of 10+ seconds after someone opens your post adds 0.4
- the boost favors the post with the best like rate from its first viewers
- accounts up to 50K can get one fresh original lifted to roughly 16th
- nothing beats a copy link share, it scores 20
- replies, quotes and DM shares each score 5
- talk with your mutuals, replies between you score 20 instead of 5
- originals are the only posts that travel outside your follower base
- the 1st and the 32nd like each open a new route to strangers
- your 2nd post in the same feed is worth 62% of the first, so pick your best one
- videos still need 10+ seconds to qualify for the video lists
- earning a follow adds 4
- a pinned post with a bad link can flag the account for 7 days, worth a quick check

What you should NOT be doing:

- posts that get labeled low quality or misinfo now carry a warning, and nobody outside your followers can like or share them
- video alone won't carry you, an open counts 0.02 and the watch 0
- hide-worthy posts cost more, "not interested" sits at -52.27
- a post at 3am burns its 2 hour window before anyone sees it
- a tap that turns into a bounce is worth only 0.3
- replies and reposts don't get past your followers
- insults get your post hidden from anyone who doesn't follow you
- adult media in 3 of your last 5 posts puts a label on your account
- disguised content in videos gets checked from 64 likes, harder at 512
- self-reply chains under big accounts risk being zeroed
- one account label and non-followers stop seeing you entirely
- low-rated links don't belong in your pinned post
- recycled wording can get tagged as copypasta spam
- strangers tagged plus a low quality link is a pattern X flags
- engagement bait has no size exemption
- several posts in a row end up competing with each other
- hashtag stacks add nothing
- bookmarks are still worth 0
- 48 hours in, For You is finished with a post
key_points: New posts now get a fair chance instead of being cut first.
The first 2 hours and first 200 views still decide reach.
Copy-link shares score 20; bookmarks still score 0.
Low-quality labels block likes and shares from non-followers.
action: Post your best original when your followers are online, and reply to mutuals in its first 2 hours

tldr: Felix dropped coding interviews; hunger beats tenure for juniors
summary: Felix Rieseberg says the coding interview no longer gives signal for his Anthropic team, so he removed it this month. His post argues it's a chance for junior engineers: drive and shipping now count more than years of tenure.
text:
The coding interview is dead, at least for my team at Anthropic. I've seen enough to know that it no longer provides signal. I removed it from loops this month.

I have a spicy, optimistic take - I think there's an opportunity for junior engineers: https://t.co/PVvpQCbQtK
key_points: Coding interview removed from his Anthropic loops
It no longer gives signal
Junior engineers get an opening
Hunger and shipping beat tenure
action: Write one paragraph about something you shipped out of hunger, for your next interview

tldr: An anonymous seller shares his Meta ads playbook, with red flags
summary: An anonymous founder who says he sold a luxury ecommerce business explains his Meta ads method: optimize for a custom "qualified lead" score, not purchases, and enrich leads with data brokers. He admits one step was "definitely not legal" (unmasking ad engagers); claims are unverified and raise privacy and legal red flags.
text:
Two weeks ago a life changing amount of money was wired into my bank account from the sale of my business.

Since I'm no longer a competitor in this particular arena, I'm gonna drop some sauce on how I completely mogged an entire industry on meta ads.

I'm going to be vague so I don't dox myself, but here it goes:

---

It was an old school brick and mortar business, so the first thing I did was completely redesign the business model from the ground up to focus on e-commerce.  That's been my go to way to make money for the last decade; it worked and I was happy for a couple years as the profits came in.

We were selling massive luxury items that cost between $10-20,000 per unit, to wealthy people across the country.  Margins were great- on a $15,000 unit we would profit between $3000-6000.  We were one of the first companies that figured out how to transport these cheaply and efficiently.  We were also one of the first to push professional quality video ads on meta.

After 2-3 years competitors caught on and profit dipped so I needed another innovation to keep myself ahead of the pack.  I started focusing hard on ways to reduce my customer acquisition cost, and I stumbled onto something that gave me a massive advantage.

---

Modern ad systems have always been run on machine learning algos, but in the past 5 years the trend has accelerated with AI now doing all the targeting for you.  In the past you would hire a media buyer to tweak things.  You could adjust the demographic you want to target, the exact locations, the time of day, etc...  You used to have hundreds of these levers you could a/b test and optimize.  In the past 5 years this has shifted to AI, so you don't need a media buyer anymore.  You just set a conversion target and the AI targeting systems will grind on it.

When you're selling something cheap like yoga pants, all you have to do is create good ads and set your conversion target to gross margin.  The AI will find you sales, and it will even optimize for the exact customer profile that you'll earn the most margin on.

However, when you're selling $20,000 items, you'll never hit enough of volume to properly train the ads.  You need at least 50 conversions per week so unless you're doing $1 mil revenue weekly, you can't target margin.

Instead you target something higher up the funnel like a phone call or a lead form submission.  You can even put additional qualifiers- such as the phone call needs to last at least 5 min.

What we did at first was to ask a follow up question after a customer submitted a quote request on our website-:

How were you planning to pay?

Option 1- Pay cash
Option 2- Finance with FICO over 650
Option 3- Finance with FICO under 650.

And then we simply targeted option 1 and option 2 as the reward function.  This filtered out a bunch of the poors, but we still captured the lead even if they refused to answer.  If they didn't answer the question, we would just pass them along to their quote automatically after 6 seconds, plus we had automated text and email notifications sent in case they closed out before they seen it.

This had amazing results, so I realized that the biggest lever I could pull is setting a better target for the AI to grind on.

---

What we did was start to track everything!

How many times did they view their quote?  How long did they view it for?   How many times did they add an accessory or upgrade to their quote?  How many times did they email us? call us?  text us?  Did they apply for financing?  What was the rate they were approved for?

Hell we even logged every SMS + email + call transcript from the first time they ever contacted us... then we did intent analysis on those messages to determine which words were most likely to correlate with sales.

We ended up with about 95 different data points plus intent analysis... So we ran all this data through our sales history, figured out the correlations and created a customer score based on their ability to afford the product and also their engagement quality.

We got really really good at predicting who would purchase, so I obviously set the meta conversion target to this new "qualified lead".  Since the business was seasonal, I even created a custom algo to dynamically adjust the target on the fly so we always ended up with around 50 conversions per week.  If business got slow, the algo would adjust to be less aggressive about who we considered to be a "qualified lead", and during good times it would adjust to be more aggressive.

It worked really well, but then I had another lightbulb moment and figured out a way to drastically increase the accuracy yet again...

---

Up until this point, we were only logging data from activity that occured on our website, or from the contacts between customers and the sales reps.

Then one day I learned about data brokers, and realized there was a lot of data on these customers that was external to my website.

When a customer first entered our sales funnel, we took the identifiers they voluntarily gave us and we ran them through a number of data broker APIs to dig up as much info on them as possible:

Household income
Credit Score
Gender
Age
Ethnic group
Martial status
Own or rent
Occupation
Education 
Length of year at residence
Home equity
Children in the home
Age of children
Est net worth
Home value
Auto year make model
Home market value

...and much much more.  Keep in mind this is totally legal up to this point.  All we had to do is add a couple sentences to our privacy policy that no one ever reads.  It cost like 10 cents per customer to find all this stuff out.

Now all of a sudden we had some external data to add to the algo, but of course I didn't stop there.

I realized I could go the other way and set up a custom exclusion list, based on a loss function.  Being able to predict who would buy also gave us the ability to predict who wouldn't!

We set up an automation to add those people to an exclusion list so we wouldn't waste any more money serving them ads.

At this point it starts getting into a grey area legally, and is definitely against metas terms of service.

Then I took it another step which was definitely not legal 😂, because why not.

We started paying remote workers overseas to create a database of all the people who liked or commented on our ads.  People who never went on our website or agreed to our privacy policy.

Then we used a different set of data brokers to unmask and identify these Facebook and Instagram handles.  Once we linked a handle to a real name and email address, we had another automation that would send them to the first set of data brokers to create a financial profile on them.  So about 20 seconds after they liked one of our videos the system would come back with a predictive score to determine how likely they were to afford what we were selling and if they couldn't, the system would automatically add them to an exclusion list.

---

I'm just a retard that dropped out of high school.  I figured all this out by asking AI a lot of questions.

Hopefully this helps someone out there.  There is quite a lot you can do to sculpt traffic and learn about your leads.  Data is your friend.
key_points: Optimize Meta for a custom qualified-lead event
Tune the target to about 50 conversions a week
Data-broker enrichment and exclusion lists
Admits an illegal unmasking step; do not copy
